title: Politicians have got no hope when it comes to AI
gist: Alan Rusbridger argues that legislators in the US and UK lack the technical literacy to oversee AI — echoing their failures over 2008 derivatives and Snowden-era surveillance — but that, unlike then, even AI's builders admit they don't understand their models. Drawing on Robert Dahl and the Dewey–Lippmann debate, he says democratic oversight of AI is badly compromised, with Trump focused on beating China and the stock market.

insights.claim: Congressional hearings have repeatedly exposed lawmakers' ignorance of tech, e.g. Orrin Hatch asking Mark Zuckerberg in 2018 how Facebook makes money ('Senator, we run ads'), Steve King quizzing Sundar Pichai about an iPhone, and Ted Stevens' 2006 'series of tubes' description of the internet.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: History suggests tech regulation lags and is poorly targeted — Big Tech has faced weak legislative constraint.
insights.locator: We will all have our favourite moments.

insights.claim: Twenty years after Facebook's public launch, legislators are still struggling to decide how, or even whether, to regulate social media.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: If social media regulation took two decades without resolution, comprehensive AI regulation is likely to lag far behind deployment.

insights.claim: In 2008 few MPs, regulators or bank boards understood the derivatives that crashed the global economy, and after Snowden in 2013 lawmakers had no real grasp of bulk collection or metadata; expertise sat almost exclusively inside the firms and agencies themselves.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Pattern of expertise concentrated in the regulated entity is a known precursor to systemic risk going unchecked.

insights.claim: Asked by Rusbridger, ChatGPT identified only one of 650 MPs — Dr Allison Gardner, with a PhD in computational biology — with the expertise to interrogate AI companies, plus Lord Lionel Tarassenko in the Lords; Claude identified just four members of Congress who might be equipped.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Extremely thin legislative AI expertise makes AI firms the de facto setters of their own rules.

insights.claim: Some AI creators argue the technology carries a 10 per cent chance of wiping out humanity within a decade, yet democratic leaders still struggle with TikTok.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Mismatch between stated risk and oversight capacity is a latent regulatory shock risk.
insights.quote: comes with a 10 per cent chance of wiping out humanity itself within a decade

insights.claim: Unlike banks in 2008 or spies in 2013, AI insiders themselves don't fully understand their creations; Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in 2025 that this lack of understanding is essentially unprecedented in the history of technology.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Neither regulators nor developers can fully assess model failure modes — raising tail risk for AI-exposed firms.
insights.quote: this lack of understanding is essentially unprecedented in the history of technology

insights.claim: Robert Dahl's 1985 book Controlling Nuclear Weapons parallels the AI debate: complex specialised knowledge, catastrophic mistakes, and citizens unable to master the details; Dahl rejected expert 'guardianship' because experts aren't reliably benevolent or equipped for moral judgments.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Expert-led AI governance carries legitimacy and capture risks; democratic oversight requires competence that is lacking.

insights.claim: Dahl conceded that decisions of incalculable importance had been handed to a small group and it was unclear how control could be recaptured — a description Rusbridger implies now fits AI.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Control over AI trajectory is effectively concentrated among a handful of firms.
insights.quote: We have in fact turned over to a small group of people decisions of incalculable importance to ourselves and mankind

insights.claim: The 1920s Dewey–Lippmann debate — whether the press can create an informed public capable of democratic deliberation, or the modern world is too complex for it — recurs with AI, only worse.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Public understanding is unlikely to catch up fast enough to discipline AI policy.

insights.claim: Rusbridger says Trump is clueless about AI and treats it as about beating the Chinese and boosting the stock market, rather than managing catastrophic risk.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: US AI policy is likely to remain pro-acceleration and market-supportive, favouring AI capex beneficiaries over safety constraints.
insights.quote: For Trump, it’s all about beating the Chinese and fluffing the stock market.

insights.claim: Better-informed lawmakers are urgently needed, but so are philosophers, historians and political scientists to grapple with language, oversight, control and democracy in AI.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Signals a growing constituency for AI governance capacity-building.
insights.quote: Don’t close down those humanities departments just yet.
